video_title: High Yields To Pull Asset Prices Down | Danielle Park
gist: Danielle Park argues the 130bp surge in the US 10-year to ~5.3% and the end of zero-rate policy are exposing leveraged households, second-home owners and richly valued, narrowly led equities, with housing, credit spreads and the 2007-like indicators pointing to a prolonged correction. Her playbook is to rebalance toward short-duration bonds (3-5 years), later add corporate debt and duration once cuts start; New Harbor's Preston and Lodra broadly agree on de-risking but dispute her view on gold and whether policy allows a clean reset.

insights.claim: The US 10-year Treasury yield has risen about 130bp in seven months to ~5.3%, versus roughly 80bp gains at the peaks of the 2000, 2007 and 2022 cycles that were enough to trigger risk corrections; she argues speed of change (a ~10x rise from the 2020 low), not the level, is what hurts leveraged borrowers.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Rate-of-change comparisons to prior cycle peaks frame the current move as already past correction-trigger thresholds.
insights.quote: we've now seen 130 beeps of increase in seven months

insights.claim: Park views the return of positive rates as net constructive: it ends malinvestment, forces fiscal and corporate discipline, restores savers' yields and dividend/deposit income, and should be disinflationary, while hurting only the indebted and speculators.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: A contrarian-to-consensus read that higher rates are a cleansing mechanism, not just a headwind.
insights.quote: now we're in a period where math matters and um compensation for capital is back

insights.claim: She rejects the popular US-deficit explanation for rising yields, arguing the move is global and driven mainly by the Iran-war oil spike (diesel near $10, gasoline above $4) and inflation fear; Japan, China and Canada carry heavier debt or deficits yet have much lower yields.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: If oil, not fiscal supply, drives yields, an oil reversal or demand destruction could pull yields down fast.

insights.claim: Canada's 1990s precedent: after years of rising deficits and the Mexican peso crisis, a credit downgrade spiked rates and forced deep spending cuts across all levels; ratings recovered and Canada ran surpluses until the GFC. Park's point is that discipline usually requires a crisis.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Template for how bond-market pressure forces fiscal retrenchment, relevant to US deficit debate.

insights.claim: US growth above 3% despite fast rate increases is explained by lagged effects, AI data-center construction multipliers (chips and equipment are mostly imported), and above all a self-fulfilling stock market supporting high-end consumption and cheap capital for tech.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: The economy's resilience leans on equity wealth effects, so an equity drawdown transmits quickly to spending.

insights.claim: About 12% of Canadian mortgages remain up for renewal in 2027 facing roughly a 15% payment increase (Bank of Canada estimate), and Canadian mortgage defaults have already doubled from the 2022 low; US refinance applications were down 56% year over year in September.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Canadian short-term mortgage resets preview the US lock-in unwinding, with delinquencies the lagging signal.

insights.claim: Canadian real home prices are down about 29% (20% nominal) from the peak yet still 35% above 2019; US average prices are 54% above 2019. Price-to-income is 5.2x in the US, 8.9x in Canada and about 10x in Toronto and Vancouver, so she argues 'down 20%' is not enough and more downside is needed.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Affordability math, not drawdown from peak, defines the bottom; expect continued price pressure even if rates fall.

insights.claim: China is treated as the leading indicator for the housing cycle: six years into falling real prices with ~3% mortgage rates, which Park uses to argue Canada's 4.6 years of declines have further to run and that the problem is price level, not rates.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Housing adjustments typically run 5 to 7 years, implying a few more years of weakness in Canada and the US.

insights.claim: Roughly 30% of Americans are over 55, own over half of housing, and one in five of them owns multiple properties; aging second-home owners with unsellable cottages and chalets are a latent supply wave, with GTA listings cut 30-40% and some halved without selling.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Demographic supply overhang is the answer to 'where will supply come from' and weighs on prices into spring.

insights.claim: Delistings by sellers waiting for spring ('rage delisting', a term attributed to Melody Wright) are not evidence of strength; Park expects more listings by spring as holding costs and winter carry wear sellers down, and the Airbnb/short-term-rental bust returns rental supply, cutting Canadian asking rents almost 5%.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Falling rents hit shelter, a third to 40% of CPI, so housing weakness is disinflationary.

insights.claim: Park downplays immigration cuts as a housing driver: revised Canadian data show immigration held up better than thought, and new immigrants rarely buy in their first few years, so the effect shows in rents rather than home prices.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Policy-driven demand shock is likely overstated for home prices.

insights.claim: Park sees many indicators lining up with the 2007 peak: consumer confidence, unemployment levels, rising delinquencies, and multiple job holders back at cycle highs as households work extra to service debt; unemployment is a lagging indicator that would amplify forced downsizing if it rises.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Credit stress is appearing before the labor-market headline, so jobs data may confirm late.

insights.claim: She warns against extrapolating oil and inflation: high commodity prices seed their own reversal via demand suppression, supply response and EV/hybrid shifts (about 60% of Chinese auto purchases electric), so she expects a more muted inflation outcome than consensus higher-rate views.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: If oil rolls over after the Iran spike, the 'rates to the moon' trade could reverse.

insights.claim: AI is late-cycle in Park's view: AI companies spend ever more while revenue per user weakens, and cheap capital incentivizes overbuilding supply just as pricing is pressured.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Capex outpacing monetization is the classic setup for an investment-cycle bust.

insights.claim: US market concentration now exceeds the 2000 peak (Microsoft and GE at 9% of S&P then); Park says Nvidia and Meta are holding the index up while breadth is terrible: 70% of stocks down 10%, 60% down 20%, and the S&P ex-AI-leaders negative since August.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Index highs overstate market health; leadership narrowness raises fragility.

insights.claim: Equity risk premium (forward earnings minus 10-year yield) hit an all-time low, with S&P dividend yield about 1%, Dow 1.3% and TSX 2%, versus 5%-plus contractual bond income; the CAPE is above 41 versus 35 a year ago. One-year forward returns stayed positive despite her earlier warning, but she says it speaks poorly for 3, 5 and 10 years.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Stocks offer principal risk with minimal income, so bond competition becomes the marginal-flow driver.

insights.claim: Bitcoin is used as a risk-appetite barometer: it halved, bounced, and is weak again; Park's thesis is it was enabled by free money and permissive policy, and that tech, which holds up the S&P and high-end spending, could follow its lead.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Crypto weakness as a lead signal for tech and the wealth-effect chain.

insights.claim: The TSX looks vulnerable despite little tech: financials are about 37% of the index (versus a usual 32-33%), Canadian banks are at record relative valuations to US banks (which have fallen since August), and higher-for-longer hurts bank earnings through weaker loan demand, fewer capital-markets deals and defaults. The TSX also topped just after the NASDAQ in 2000.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Canada offers little diversification when the global risk trade unwinds.

insights.claim: Diversification across regions and equity sectors fails at turning points: Canada, Japan, Germany and the S&P equal-weight all fall together, and low dividend yields give only a small cushion; US, Japan and Canada all have market caps over 200% of GDP, so Buffett-indicator mean reversion would be global.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: In a risk-off event, equity diversification is weak; real protection must come from asset class and duration choices.

themes.theme: Credit, bonds and the Fed cycle

insights.claim: High-yield and CCC spreads are back to 2022 widths and CCC-vs-BB spread differentials are the widest since the mid-1990s per Lodra, which he reads as stress at the periphery that historically cascades into higher quality, though 'not an alarm bell yet'. Investment grade has not repriced yet, with about $1.4 trillion of IG debt to be refinanced by 2030.
insights.speaker: John Lodra, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Credit spreads are the early-warning canary; the IG refinancing wall could curtail buybacks and M&A.

insights.claim: Higher funding costs end the buyback-driven loop where corporates lowered their cost of capital by repurchasing shares with free money; Park says rate discipline has 'put a spike in the gears' of buybacks and M&A.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: A key equity demand source weakens as borrowing costs normalize.

insights.claim: Historically stocks outperform bonds for a decade into a peak, then bonds beat stocks as yields rise and stocks fall, and investors rotate to bonds at the wrong time. Treasuries have already mean-reverted in price, while stocks have not, and the worst stock carnage tends to occur once the Fed starts cutting, as central banks chase markets down.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: A Fed pivot is a symptom of equity stress, not a green light to buy stocks.

insights.claim: Markets have priced in four potential Fed hikes over the next year (cuts were expected in February), but Park expects an eventual return to cutting if oil falls from Middle East resolution before US midterms or demand destruction.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Rate-path surprise risk is skewed toward cuts if oil falls.

insights.claim: Park's bond positioning: avoid long duration for now (20-year Treasury at ~4.2% because older low-coupon bonds), run portfolio duration of 3-5 years, shift from stocks to short bonds, and wait to buy corporate debt once it reprices; later extend duration and rotate into beaten-up dividend payers when cuts start.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: A sequenced playbook: reweight, short duration, credit after repricing, then duration and dividend stocks.

insights.claim: Park says people at or near retirement should hold far less than 60-70% in equities, more like 30%, and notes bond allocations are near historic lows as at the 1999 and 2007 tops; most investors have not rebalanced after the run-up. With boomers all over 65 within three years she calls it a 'fragile decade'.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Sequence-of-returns risk and record equity weights imply forced de-risking by older cohorts.

insights.claim: Park expects the equity adjustment to be longer than the sharp, quick drawdowns of 2007-09 and 2022 if real rates stay positive and central banks are constrained; returns over 3 to 10 years from current valuations could be negative, citing 15 years to recover after 2000 and six or seven years for Canada after 2008.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Policy response (QE) is the key wild card for whether this is a V or a decade-long grind.

insights.claim: Term premium has risen from about -0.6% in 2020 to above 1%, close to its long-term average, and Lodra says the 10-year could still rise another 50bp toward ~6% but that much negative sentiment and policy extremes are priced in; New Harbor's fixed income duration is about 4.3 years.
insights.speaker: John Lodra, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Term premium normalization suggests the repricing of duration is largely done but not necessarily over.

insights.claim: Crowded bond pessimism: eight or nine of ten New Harbor clients are worried about bonds and only 10-15% see yields as an opportunity, which Preston reads as one-sided sentiment that often precedes a reversal, with policymakers likely to act to cap rates; they hold ~7.5% in long Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Contrarian sentiment signal for a bond bounce.

themes.theme: Gold and silver: bubble or pullback

insights.claim: Park says gold has behaved as a risk asset: it surged into January on ETF/product proliferation and retail piling in, and she sees it and silver still overbought on long-term monthly RSI; silver's 2011 and gold's 1980 tops are cited as warnings, and she finds it inconsistent that gold bulls cheer central bank buying while calling central banks incompetent.
insights.speaker: Danielle Park, portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Narrative-driven product launches mark tops; zero-rate culture inflated demand for non-yielding alternatives.

insights.claim: Preston counters that gold (~$4,100, down 30-35% from the peak) and silver (~$60, down 50%+) are in an eight-to-nine-month pullback not unusual historically; he recommends 5-10% physical metals and says silver needs to clear ~$74 and gold ~$4,500-4,600 to confirm a bottom.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Defined technical levels for confirming a gold/silver bottom.

themes.theme: New Harbor risk management and global value

insights.claim: New Harbor cut equity exposure from about 50% to 39% after stops triggered on regional banks, REITs and S&P equal weight, signaling that the market narrowness is already being traded defensively; Preston urges passive investors to reduce from 70-80% stocks to about 30%.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Rules-based exits from cyclical sectors are firing even as the index is at highs.

insights.claim: Lodra suspects the cleansing 'reset' Park hopes for may not happen: policymakers will double down with QE or yield control, potentially triggering runaway inflation, so the outcome is a spasmodic, tumultuous path rather than a clean forest-fire burn.
insights.speaker: John Lodra, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Fiscal and monetary dominance means resets may be delayed and ultimately inflationary.

insights.claim: Valuation dispersion: US large-cap CAPE is 40.5 (99th percentile) versus Brazil in the 26th percentile; New Harbor sees Latin America (Brazil breakout on election expectations, Chile) as an area to take risk, while acknowledging a global risk-off would hit everywhere.
insights.speaker: John Lodra, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Relative-value shift toward cheaper non-US markets as a hedge against US multiple compression.

insights.claim: VIX near 15 means index put protection is still cheap; Lodra notes that buying strikes further below the market is like a bigger deductible and lowers the premium.
insights.speaker: John Lodra, New Harbor Financial
insights.so_what: Cheap implied vol is an opportunity to hedge stretched valuations.
